k-1.x_notes: Problems 1, 2, 4 and 5 are the same as Y's and are sound. P1 mixes coverable shapes with an odd-area trapezoid, a side-2 triangle and an even-area but unbalanced trapezoid. P2 is fewest greens on triangles of side 2-4. P4 is fewest blocks with the mixed set. In the P5 blue-block game, 1,2,1,1,2 is correct for strips of 4,5,6,7 triangles and the hexagon. Boards are actual size and the pages are clean, with no filler. Its main difference is P6, where the 1-2-2 hexagon is printed six times at actual size so children build every way with blocks and compare the boards side by side. That is fully hands-on and right for kindergartners. The weakness is that P3 (2 hexagons, 3 elongated hexagons) and P6 (6 boards) print exactly as many boards as there are tilings, so the 'find all' count is given away. P6 runs onto a mostly empty page 7 and needs about 30 blue blocks per child. P5 uses the numerals 1/2, which pre-readers can follow.
k-1.y_notes: P1, P2, P4 and P5 match X apart from labels; P5 has the words 'first/second', which young children need read to them. In P3, Y prints more boards than there are tilings (3 hexagons for 2 ways, 4 elongated hexagons for 3 ways). That keeps 'find all' honest and lets an adult raise 'can you find another?'. P6 has one actual-size board for building and eight half-size hexagons for drawing the 6 ways. This keeps the count open and leaves a record to compare and share. The cost is that kindergartners must draw rhombus tilings on small half-scale grids, which is hard for their fine motor skills and takes them away from the blocks. They will probably need adult help with every drawing.
k-1.reason: The packets are nearly identical. X's P6 keeps the K-1 children building with blocks on actual-size boards instead of drawing on half-size grids, which suits kindergartners better. Y's surplus boards are the more honest 'find all' design, which keeps the preference slight.

grades-2-3.x_notes: This is a strong, correct sequence. P1 has a star that can be covered, a side-3 triangle, an even-area trapezoid with 7 up and 5 down triangles, and a coverable hexagon. P2 removes two up-triangles in E (impossible), uses vertex-touching triangles in F (balanced but impossible) and removes one up and one down in G (possible). P3 asks for fewest greens on triangles of side 2-5 and why side 5 needs 5. P4 compares chevrons with blues in a table. P5 asks for a 19-triangle board needing 5 greens; it can be solved by adding a down and two up-triangles to the side-4 triangle, so it is accessible. P6 asks for a rule for two greens on the side-2 hexagon; I checked all 144 up/down pairs and every one can be covered, so the clean rule is 'one up, one down'. It has enough work for 40 minutes, and the P3 prompt points children to the next page. Weakness: it never asks children to generalize to n directly.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Everything in X is here, plus a short P4 asking for the fewest greens on triangles of side 10 and side 100. That is the kernel's general statement, reached right after the concrete table, with almost no extra reading. The design problem becomes 20 triangles needing at least 6 greens. That is still feasible (13 up and 7 down triangles, for example a comb along a row) but cannot be reached by patching the side-4 triangle. It is harder and deeper, though some third graders may need adult help. Small weakness: P3 no longer says the biggest triangle is on the next page.
grades-2-3.reason: The packets are the same except for Y's generalization question and its harder design problem. Both push the third graders toward the real idea (up minus down equals n) without adding filler. X's easier design problem keeps this from being more than slight.

grades-4-5.x_notes: This is a rich, correct development. P1 is all 6 tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon, with 10 boards so the count is not given away. P2 is the flip graph. P3 asks for shortest flip routes; I checked the printed pairs: A to B takes 3, C to D takes 4, and E to F takes 8 (the two extreme tilings). P4 is the 4-cycle question with the 5 and 7 parity question; covering A does lie on a 4-cycle, so the task can be done. P5 introduces ribbons, P6 asks for proofs of parity and the lower bound, and P7 and P8 are counts (20 tilings each). In P2, children label their P1 coverings with letters and draw the graph freely in open space, with no redrawing and room to arrange the diamond-shaped graph. P4 names a specific starting covering, so the group shares one concrete task. Small weaknesses: the P2 letters can be confused with P3's A-F, and the P5 wording calls the P3 board 'the hexagon board' although P1's board is also a hexagon.
grades-4-5.y_notes: The content and diagrams are the same as X's and are correct. P2 makes children redraw all six coverings on eight small boards and connect them with lines. That is copying busywork, and the fixed grid of boards makes the graph harder to lay out clearly. It does put the pictures next to the graph. P4 lets children start from any covering, which is more open but less concrete: a child who picks an extreme tiling has only one possible flip and cannot make a 4-cycle from it. The shared wording issue in P5 is also here.
grades-4-5.reason: The packets are identical apart from P2 and P4. X's letter graph avoids redrawing six tilings and gives the 4-5 children room to arrange the flip graph. Its named starting covering is concrete and verified to work.

overall.reason: The two packets share almost all their problems and diagrams, and both are mathematically correct and well sequenced, so every difference is small. X is slightly better for K-1 (building with blocks instead of drawing on small grids) and for grades 4-5 (no redrawing busywork in the flip-graph problem). Y's generalization question gives it a slight edge for grades 2-3, which is not enough to outweigh X's advantages in the other two bands.
